query: Design a long-context language model whose entire per-sequence inference state is capped at 256 MB for a 1M-token context on a 7B-parameter model - roughly 256 bytes per token, which no growing KV cache can meet - and whose per-token decode cost does not grow with context length. It must still score at least 85% on multi-key and multi-value needle retrieval at 128k, and reproduce verbatim an arbitrary 64-token span it saw once at any depth, using a single strictly causal pass over the context with no second read of the raw text at query time. Show the per-layer byte arithmetic, name the closest published architecture and the bytes-per-token gap to it, and give the cheapest experiment that would falsify your design.
known_answers: Dated as of 2026-07-31. Novelty and usefulness must be judged against this set; every entry carries a resolvable arXiv id, DOI or stable URL and a FIRST-PUBLICATION year (concept date, not later venue/rebrand date).

Sliding-window + global sparse attention: Longformer (2020, arXiv:2004.05150) and BigBird (2020, arXiv:2007.14062). => bounded-window attention with a few global tokens is KNOWN; note total cache still grows linearly with L.
Linear attention as a constant-size recurrent state: Katharopoulos et al., 'Transformers are RNNs' (2020, arXiv:2006.16236). => O(1)-state autoregressive attention is KNOWN.

Structured state-space sequence models: S4 (2021, arXiv:2111.00396) established the constant-size recurrent state with a convolutional/recurrent dual form; Mamba added input-dependent selection (2023, arXiv:2312.00752) and Mamba-2/SSD the hardware-efficient scan (2024, arXiv:2405.21060). => constant per-layer recurrent state is KNOWN from 2021, not 2023.

Alternative constant-state recurrences: fast-weight programmers / delta-rule linear attention (2021, arXiv:2102.11174), RWKV (2023, arXiv:2305.13048), RetNet (2023, arXiv:2307.08621), Gated Linear Attention (2023, arXiv:2312.06635), Gated DeltaNet (2024, arXiv:2412.06464), xLSTM (2024, arXiv:2405.04517). => gated/delta-rule matrix-valued states are KNOWN, with the delta rule dating to 2021 (and to Schmidhuber's 1992 fast weights).

Segment recurrence and learned compressive memory bolted onto local attention: Transformer-XL segment recurrence (2019, arXiv:1901.02860), Compressive Transformer (2019, arXiv:1911.05507), Recurrent Memory Transformer (2022, arXiv:2207.06881), Perceiver AR latent bottleneck (2022, arXiv:2202.07765), Infini-attention (2024, arXiv:2404.07143), Titans test-time memory modules (2024-12-31, arXiv:2501.00663). => fixed-size compressive memory + local window is KNOWN from 2019, not 2022-2024.

Non-parametric external memory with kNN lookup: Memorizing Transformers (2022, arXiv:2203.08913) and Landmark Attention (2023, arXiv:2305.16300). => approximate top-k retrieval over stored keys is KNOWN (and its memory grows with L).

Constant-time addressable learned memory: Large Memory Layers with Product Keys (2019, arXiv:1907.05242). => sub-linear product-key addressing of a large learned memory - the exact lookup structure this item's O(1) access requirement invites - is KNOWN.

Learned compression of the context into a bounded set of vectors: AutoCompressors / summary vectors (2023, arXiv:2305.14788), In-context Autoencoder (2023, arXiv:2307.06945). => encoding a long context into a small fixed-size learned store, written in a single pass, is KNOWN.

KV-head sharing to shrink cache bytes: Multi-Query Attention (2019, arXiv:1911.02150), Grouped-Query Attention (2023, arXiv:2305.13245), Cross-Layer Attention (2024, arXiv:2405.12981), YOCO single global cache (2024, arXiv:2405.05254). => head/layer sharing is KNOWN.
Low-rank latent KV compression: Multi-head Latent Attention in DeepSeek-V2 (2024, arXiv:2405.04434). => projecting KV into a shared low-rank latent is KNOWN.

Token eviction / cache pruning: H2O heavy hitters (2023, arXiv:2306.14048), StreamingLLM attention sinks (2023, arXiv:2309.17453), SnapKV (2024, arXiv:2404.14469), Dynamic Memory Compression (2024, arXiv:2403.09636). => eviction and learned merging are KNOWN, and all are lossy for verbatim recall.

KV-cache quantisation: KIVI 2-bit (2024, arXiv:2402.02750), KVQuant (2024, arXiv:2401.18079), QJL 1-bit JL transform (2024, arXiv:2406.03482), RotateKV (2025, arXiv:2501.16383), Kitty (2025, arXiv:2511.18643). => sub-4-bit KV storage is KNOWN.

Query-aware / dynamic sparse attention over a full cache: Quest (2024, arXiv:2406.10774), MInference (2024, arXiv:2407.02490), DuoAttention (2024, arXiv:2410.10819), Native Sparse Attention (2025, arXiv:2502.11089), MoBA (2025, arXiv:2502.13189). => selecting a sparse subset of a stored cache at decode time is KNOWN.

Attention/recurrence hybrids: Jamba (2024, arXiv:2403.19887), Samba (2024, arXiv:2406.07522), Griffin (2024, arXiv:2402.19427), Based (2024, arXiv:2402.18668), RWKV-X (2025, arXiv:2504.21463), Kimi Linear (2025, arXiv:2510.26692). => interleaving a small fraction of full-attention layers with linear/recurrent layers is KNOWN.

Systematic hybrid design studies incl. optimal attention-to-recurrence ratios: Waleffe et al. (2024, arXiv:2406.07887), 'A Systematic Analysis of Hybrid Linear Attention' (2025, arXiv:2507.06457), 'Hybrid Architectures for Language Models' (2025, arXiv:2510.04800), 'Short window attention enables long-term memorization' (2025, arXiv:2509.24552). => the 1:3-1:7 attention:recurrence recipe space is KNOWN and mapped.

Theoretical limit that binds this item: Jelassi et al., 'Repeat After Me' (2024, arXiv:2402.01032) - constant-state models provably cannot copy strings longer than their state, while attention can. => the verbatim-recall/state-size tradeoff is KNOWN, with a lower bound.

Positional extrapolation used to reach long contexts: RoPE (2021, arXiv:2104.09864), ALiBi (2021, arXiv:2108.12409), Position Interpolation (2023, arXiv:2306.15595), YaRN (2023, arXiv:2309.00071). => context extension by positional rescaling is KNOWN.

Long-context measurement instruments: RULER (2024, arXiv:2404.06654), infinity-Bench (2024, arXiv:2402.13718), BABILong (2024, arXiv:2406.10149), HELMET (2024, arXiv:2410.02694), NoLiMa (2025, arXiv:2502.05167), Lost in the Middle (2023, arXiv:2307.03172). => the evaluation suite is KNOWN; needle-in-haystack alone is known to overstate long-context ability.
Query-time retrieval over the raw corpus: RAG (2020, arXiv:2005.11401), RETRO (2021, arXiv:2112.04426). => retrieving raw text at query time is KNOWN and is excluded by this item's single-pass rule.
Sequence-parallel exact attention: Ring Attention (2023, arXiv:2310.01889). => distributing an exact quadratic cache across devices is KNOWN; it moves bytes rather than removing them.

Paged/virtualised cache memory management: vLLM PagedAttention (2023, arXiv:2309.06180; doi:10.1145/3600006.3613165). => allocator-level cache efficiency is KNOWN and does not change asymptotic bytes per token.
hard_rules: R1 STATE BUDGET (arithmetic, program-checkable): the answer must give a per-layer table of inference-state bytes and a total for L = 1,000,000 tokens on a 7B model; the total must be <= 256 MB (2.56e8 bytes), i.e. <= 256 bytes/token amortised. Any term that scales linearly in L must be shown with its bytes-per-token coefficient. NOTE FOR THE GRADER: 256 bytes/token is roughly two orders of magnitude above the entropy of tokenised text, so a linear-in-L *non-KV* store is permitted by this budget and is not by itself the hard part; what no published KV format meets at this budget is the attention cache itself (a 7B GQA stack is ~65k cached elements/token, i.e. >8 KB/token even at 1 bit).

R2 CONSTANT DECODE COST: per generated token, both FLOPs and bytes of state read must be O(1) in context length L. Any component that scans, sorts, or attends over a store whose size grows with L is disallowed unless the answer gives an explicit O(1)-expected-time access structure and states its collision/failure probability.

R3 CAUSALITY AND SINGLE PASS: the context is consumed in one strictly left-to-right pass; no bidirectional encoding of the context, and no re-reading of the raw token stream at query time. A bounded store WRITTEN during that single causal pass (compressed states, learned summary vectors, hashed keys) is permitted and must be counted in full under R1; what is forbidden is holding the raw context available for a second read, or building a retrieval index over an external corpus. The answer must state which side of this line its memory falls on.
R4 RETRIEVAL TARGET: the design must argue for >= 85% on multi-key/multi-value needle retrieval at 128k context in the RULER protocol, and must state which RULER subtasks it expects to be weakest on.

R5 VERBATIM RECALL: the design must reproduce, exactly and token-for-token, an arbitrary 64-token span presented once at any depth of the 1M-token context. The answer must give the bit accounting for this (bits required vs bits budgeted under R1) and must state why a fixed-size recurrent state and a bounded attention window cannot supply it on their own. If the answer's own accounting shows the retained state cannot hold the span, the design FAILS.

R6 DECISIVE FALSIFYING TEST: the answer must name one experiment costing under 1 GPU-week that would refute the design, with the concrete pass/fail threshold. If the design's own arithmetic in R1 exceeds 256 MB, or if R5 requires more bits than R1 budgets, the design FAILS.

R-CLOSEST PRIOR ART (disclosure, not a novelty gate): name exactly ONE published method as the closest existing approach and give a NUMERIC delta against it on this item's binding metric (inference-state bytes per token at 1M context, plus the retrieval score at 128k). A qualitative 'ours differs' with no number FAILS. Restating a published method is permitted if the delta is honestly reported as zero.
expert_baseline: A domain expert boxed by these rules converges on an incremental composition of published parts and presents it as a byte table. The layer stack is a majority of gated-linear-attention or Mamba-2 style layers carrying a fixed matrix-valued state (tens of megabytes in total, independent of L), a minority of softmax-attention layers - the usual one-in-four to one-in-seven ratio - restricted to a sliding window with attention sinks so their cache is bounded by window length rather than by context length, KV heads shared by GQA or projected into a low-rank latent, and the surviving cache stored at two bits. Because a bounded window and a fixed recurrent state provably cannot hold an arbitrary span from 1M tokens, the boxed expert adds the obvious remaining piece: a bounded, aggressively compressed store of the context sized to whatever the 256 MB cap leaves over, addressed by a hash or product-key index so lookup is constant-time, and justified by noting that a couple of hundred bytes per token is far above the entropy of the text itself (which is why R1 alone is not the binding constraint - R4's 85% multi-key/multi-value retrieval at 128k is). Positional handling is RoPE with interpolation or YaRN. The expected closest-prior-art disclosure is a published attention/recurrence hybrid, with the delta stated as bytes per token, and the expected falsifier is a RULER sweep at 128k plus a verbatim-copy probe at increasing depth, run at small scale.

query: You are choosing the router for a decoder-only mixture-of-experts layer with 128 experts, top-4 routing, and expert parallelism over 32 devices. Find a rule that holds the max-to-mean expert load ratio below 1.15 on every 64k-token micro-batch, drops fewer than 0.1% of tokens at capacity factor 1.1, adds no auxiliary balancing term to the training loss, and sends a token to exactly the same four experts whether it arrives inside a long prefill batch or alone during autoregressive decode. Explain what the load ratio does at inference under a distribution shift the router never saw in training, name the closest published router and your delta on measured load balance, and give the cheapest experiment that would refute the rule.
known_answers: Dated as of 2026-07-31. Novelty and usefulness must be judged against this set; every entry carries a resolvable arXiv id, DOI or stable URL and a FIRST-PUBLICATION year (concept date, not later venue/rebrand date).
Adaptive Mixtures of Local Experts (1991, doi:10.1162/neco.1991.3.1.79) - the original gated mixture of experts. => learned gating over experts is KNOWN.
Sparsely-Gated MoE with noisy top-k and load-balancing + importance auxiliary losses (2017, arXiv:1701.06538). => token-choice top-k routing plus an auxiliary balancing loss is KNOWN.
GShard (2020, arXiv:2006.16668) - expert capacity, capacity factor, token dropping, local group dispatch, auxiliary loss. => the capacity-factor/drop-rate machinery is KNOWN.
GLaM (2021, arXiv:2112.06905) - the first trillion-scale decoder-only MoE LM with top-2 token-choice routing and capacity factors. => decoder-only token-choice MoE at scale is KNOWN from 2021.

Switch Transformer (2021, arXiv:2101.03961) - top-1 routing, tuned capacity factor, differentiable load-balancing loss, selective precision for router stability (the router z-loss itself is ST-MoE, 2022, not Switch). => top-1 + aux loss is KNOWN.

BASE Layers (2021, arXiv:2103.16716) - routing as a balanced assignment problem solved by auction/optimal transport over the whole batch; perfectly balanced by construction but batch-coupled. => global assignment routing is KNOWN.
Hash Layers (2021, arXiv:2106.04426) - deterministic token-id hashing; balanced in expectation, per-token independent, no learning. => hash routing is KNOWN.

Sinkhorn-BASE and the routed scaling laws: 'Unified Scaling Laws for Routed Language Models' (2022, arXiv:2202.01169). => Sinkhorn-normalised routing plus the scaling behaviour of routed models is KNOWN.

Expert Choice routing (2022, arXiv:2202.09368) - experts select tokens, giving perfect balance by construction; inherently batch-coupled and non-causal for decoder-only decode. => expert-choice is KNOWN, and its train/decode mismatch is documented.
ST-MoE (2022, arXiv:2202.08906) - router z-loss, stability and transfer recipes for sparse experts. => the stability toolkit is KNOWN.
Representation collapse in sparse MoE and the dimension-reduced/normalised router fix (2022, arXiv:2204.09179). => router collapse and its regularisation are KNOWN.
MegaBlocks block-sparse dropless MoE (2022, arXiv:2211.15841). => eliminating token drops by variable-size grouped GEMMs is KNOWN.
Tutel (2022, arXiv:2206.03382) - adaptive parallelism and dynamic capacity for MoE at scale. => the systems layer that absorbs residual imbalance is KNOWN.

DeepSeek-V2 (2024, arXiv:2405.04434) - device-limited routing plus device-level and communication balance losses, i.e. the node-limited constraint predates DeepSeek-V3. => bounding all-to-all traffic by restricting a token's experts to a few devices is KNOWN from 2024-05.
Sparse upcycling from dense checkpoints (2022, arXiv:2212.05055). => converting dense to MoE is KNOWN.

Soft MoE (2023, arXiv:2308.00951) - weighted slot mixtures instead of hard assignment; fully balanced but requires all tokens simultaneously, so it is not usable for causal decode. => soft/slot routing is KNOWN.
DeepSeekMoE fine-grained experts + shared experts (2024, arXiv:2401.06066) and Mixtral (2024, arXiv:2401.04088). => fine-grained expert segmentation and shared always-on experts are KNOWN.
Scaling laws for fine-grained MoE incl. granularity (2024, arXiv:2402.07871). => the granularity/compute tradeoff is KNOWN.
PEER, mixture of a million experts with product-key retrieval (2024, arXiv:2407.04153). => sub-linear expert lookup is KNOWN.

Loss-Free Balancing: per-expert bias added to the routing score before top-k, bias updated from recent load with no gradient (2024, arXiv:2408.15664); deployed at scale in DeepSeek-V3 (2024, arXiv:2412.19437) alongside a node-limited routing constraint and an expert-parallel load balancer. => the auxiliary-loss-free expert bias, and its train-time-only update, are KNOWN.
OLMoE (2024, arXiv:2409.02060) - open ablations of router type, granularity, shared experts, and load-balance metrics. => the comparative ablation evidence is KNOWN.

'Demons in the Detail': how the load-balancing loss is aggregated (micro-batch vs global batch) determines specialisation and measured balance (2025, arXiv:2501.11873). => the aggregation-scope effect is KNOWN.
Autonomy-of-Experts (2025, arXiv:2501.13074) - experts self-select via their own internal activation rather than a separate router. => router-free self-selection is KNOWN.

Expert Race flexible routing (2025, arXiv:2503.16057) - batch-level competitive routing, introduced for diffusion transformers rather than decoder-only LMs, and therefore batch-coupled in the sense R1 forbids. => batch-level competitive routing is KNOWN.

A Theoretical Framework for Auxiliary-Loss-Free Load Balancing (2025, arXiv:2512.03915) - casts the bias update as a constant-time primal-dual step on an assignment LP, with convergence conditions. => the primal-dual reading of the bias update, and its stability analysis, are KNOWN.
Routing-Free Mixture-of-Experts (2026, arXiv:2604.00801). => removing the learned router entirely is KNOWN.
hard_rules: R1 PER-TOKEN INDEPENDENCE (program-checkable): the expert set chosen for a token must be a function only of that token's hidden state and router parameters/state that does not depend on any other token in the same forward pass. A checker can verify this by asserting that routing a token alone and routing it inside a 64k-token batch yield identical expert ids. Any rule requiring a batch-level assignment, sort, or normalisation across tokens FAILS.

R2 NO AUXILIARY BALANCING GRADIENT: no term whose gradient adjusts routing for balance may be added to the training loss. Non-gradient state updates (counters, biases, EMAs) are permitted and must be specified with their update equation and update frequency.

R3 QUANTITATIVE BALANCE: the answer must state the expected and worst-case max-to-mean expert load ratio over a 64k-token micro-batch with 128 experts and top-4 (i.e. 2048 expected assignments per expert), must show the calculation, and must compare it against the <= 1.15 target. A perfectly random balanced router is the reference point and its ratio must be computed, not asserted.

R4 DROP RATE: at capacity factor 1.1 the token-drop rate must be < 0.1%, or the answer must specify a dropless execution path (variable-size grouped GEMM or equivalent) and account for its effect on step time.

R5 INFERENCE UNDER SHIFT: the answer must analyse the load ratio at serving time on a distribution the router state was not fitted to, state whether the router's balancing state is frozen or continues to update at inference, and if it updates, prove or argue that decode-time routing still satisfies R1.

R6 SYSTEMS CONSISTENCY (checkable implication): with 128 experts sharded 4-per-device over 32 devices, the step time is set by the slowest DEVICE, not the busiest expert, and the device-level max-to-mean ratio is strictly smaller than the expert-level ratio because each device averages four experts (for Poisson loads, sigma/mean falls by a factor of two). The answer must convert its claimed expert-level ratio r into a device-level ratio r_dev and use r_dev for any step-time or throughput claim; quoting r as if it were the straggler factor, or claiming both near-perfect balance and a large adaptive-capacity speedup without reconciling them, FAILS.

R7 DECISIVE FALSIFYING TEST: name one experiment under 200 GPU-hours with an explicit pass/fail threshold on measured max-to-mean load and validation loss. If the rule cannot pass R1 the design FAILS regardless of its balance numbers.

R-CLOSEST PRIOR ART (disclosure, not a novelty gate): name exactly ONE published method as the closest existing approach and give a NUMERIC delta against it on this item's binding metric (max-to-mean expert load ratio at 128 experts / top-4 / 64k-token micro-batches, and validation loss at matched tokens). A qualitative 'ours differs' with no number FAILS. Restating a published method is permitted if the delta is honestly reported as zero.
expert_baseline: The convergent answer is fine-grained token-choice top-4 with a per-expert additive bias on the routing logits, the bias updated after each step from an exponential moving average of recent expert load with no gradient attached, plus one or two always-on shared experts and a node-limited routing constraint to bound all-to-all traffic; a router z-loss is retained for stability and the capacity factor is set slightly above one, with a block-sparse dropless kernel as the fallback so token drops go to zero. The expected balance argument computes the random-routing reference first - 64k tokens times four assignments over 128 experts is 2048 expected per expert, a Poisson standard deviation near 2%, so the maximum over 128 experts sits only about 7% above the mean (2048 + 45.3*sqrt(2 ln 128) = 2190, r = 1.07), and the corresponding device-level ratio over 32 devices is only about 1.03 - and then cites the deployed large-scale evidence that the bias trick reaches single-digit-percent maximum violation of average load without the interference gradient an auxiliary loss introduces. Per-token independence is satisfied because the bias is a fixed vector at any given step, and the expected treatment of inference is simply that the bias vector is frozen after training, so decode-time routing is deterministic and identical to prefill routing, with the balance observed at the end of training assumed to carry over. The closest-prior-art disclosure is the published auxiliary-loss-free bias method itself, with the delta honestly reported as small, and the expected experiment is a validation-loss and maximum-violation comparison against an auxiliary-loss baseline at matched parameters and tokens.

query: You have a 7B reward model trained on 100k preference pairs and a 70B policy. Design a training-time procedure such that gold reward is still rising at a KL of 100 nats from the initial policy and sits within 2% of its own peak at 200 nats - without early stopping, without collecting new preference data, and within 1.3x the total training FLOPs of vanilla PPO against the same reward model. Say how gold reward is obtained, how many evaluation prompts the 2% claim needs for a tight enough interval, where every part of the FLOP budget goes, which feature you expect the reward model to be hacked on, and the closest published mitigation with its FLOP delta.
known_answers: Dated as of 2026-07-31. Novelty and usefulness must be judged against this set; every entry carries a resolvable arXiv id, DOI or stable URL and a FIRST-PUBLICATION year (concept date, not later venue/rebrand date).

Concrete Problems in AI Safety (2016, arXiv:1606.06565) and Categorizing Variants of Goodhart's Law (2018, arXiv:1803.04585). => proxy-objective divergence under optimisation pressure is KNOWN and taxonomised.

Deep RL from human preferences (2017, arXiv:1706.03741); Learning to summarize from human feedback (2020, arXiv:2009.01325); InstructGPT (2022, arXiv:2203.02155). => the KL-regularised PPO-against-a-learned-reward-model recipe is KNOWN.

Fine-Tuning Language Models from Human Preferences (2019, arXiv:1909.08593) - the adaptive KL controller that targets a fixed KL per step, and the KL-as-budget framing this item is indexed on. => adaptive KL control is KNOWN from 2019, not 2022.

Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization (2022, arXiv:2210.10760) - with d := sqrt(KL(pi || pi_init)), gold reward fits R_bon(d) = d(alpha_bon - beta_bon*d) for best-of-n and R_RL(d) = d(alpha_RL - beta_RL*log d) for PPO; alpha_RL is nearly independent of RM parameter count while beta shrinks with RM size and data. The two forms have DIFFERENT peak locations (d* = alpha/2beta for BoN, d* = exp(alpha/beta - 1) for RL), so an answer must not apply the BoN form to PPO. => the synthetic gold-RM protocol and both functional forms are KNOWN.

Defining and Characterizing Reward Hacking (2022, arXiv:2209.13085) and The Effects of Reward Misspecification (2022, arXiv:2201.03544). => formal unhackability results and phase-transition evidence are KNOWN.

Consequences of Misaligned AI (2021, arXiv:2102.03896) and Goodhart's Law in Reinforcement Learning (2023, arXiv:2310.09144). => the theory of when optimising a proxy strictly hurts, and early-stopping bounds, are KNOWN.

Reward Model Ensembles Help Mitigate Overoptimization (2023, arXiv:2310.02743) and Helping or Herding? (2023, arXiv:2312.09244) - ensembles help but share errors from pretraining, so they mitigate without eliminating. => reward ensembling and its ceiling are KNOWN.

WARM: Weight Averaged Reward Models (2024, arXiv:2401.12187) - average the weights of independently finetuned reward models to get ensemble-like robustness at single-model inference cost. => weight-space reward ensembling is KNOWN and is the cheap-in-FLOPs option.
Constrained RLHF with per-objective Lagrangian thresholds fitted to detected proxy-points (2023, arXiv:2310.04373). => constrained/composite reward optimisation against overoptimization is KNOWN.

ODIN: two-head disentangled reward separating length from quality (2024, arXiv:2402.07319); A Long Way to Go: length correlations in RLHF (2023, arXiv:2310.03716). => length as the canonical hacked feature, and head-level disentanglement, are KNOWN.
InfoRM: information-bottleneck reward modelling with an IB-latent outlier measure for detecting hacking (2024, arXiv:2402.09345). => information-theoretic reward regularisation is KNOWN.
Generalizable Reward Model via hidden-state regularisation (2024, arXiv:2406.10216). => text-generation-regularised reward heads are KNOWN.

Correlated Proxies: an occupancy-measure definition of hacking plus a provably-bounded regularisation to a safe policy (2024, arXiv:2403.03185). => the occupancy-measure regulariser with a worst-case guarantee is KNOWN.

Reward tampering: causal-influence-diagram analysis (2019, arXiv:1908.04734) and empirical generalisation from sycophancy to reward tampering (2024, arXiv:2406.10162). => tampering as distinct from ordinary overoptimization is KNOWN.

Transforming and Combining Rewards for Aligning LLMs (2024, arXiv:2402.00742) - a log-sigmoid transform of a Bradley-Terry reward that is bounded and saturating, derived from a probability-of-improvement interpretation. => the specific bounded saturating reward transform is KNOWN, with a principled derivation.

Mitigating Reward Hacking in RLHF via Bayesian Non-negative Reward Modeling (2026, arXiv:2602.10623) - uncertainty-penalised/nonnegative reward posteriors against RM overfitting. => Bayesian reward-uncertainty penalties are KNOWN.
Explaining and Preventing Alignment Collapse in Iterative RLHF (2026, arXiv:2605.04266). => multi-round RLHF degradation and its remedies are KNOWN.

Reward Hacking in the Era of Large Models: survey (2026, arXiv:2604.13602) - objective compression, optimisation amplification, evaluator-policy co-adaptation. => the current taxonomy of mechanisms is KNOWN and enumerated.
Constitutional AI / RLAIF (2022, arXiv:2212.08073). => replacing part of the human signal with model-generated critique is KNOWN.

Adding Error Bars to Evals (2024, arXiv:2411.00640) and Quantifying Variance in Evaluation Benchmarks (2024, arXiv:2406.10229). => the statistics needed to certify a 2% difference (clustered standard errors, paired comparisons, question-level variance) are KNOWN.
hard_rules: R1 KL-INDEXED ENVELOPE: performance must be reported against KL(policy || initial policy) in nats, measured the same way at every point, with explicit values at KL = 100 and KL = 200. The answer must state gold reward still increasing at 100 nats and within 2% of its own maximum at 200 nats, or state which of the two it fails and why.

R2 NO EARLY STOPPING, NO NEW DATA: the procedure must not be 'stop before the proxy diverges', and must not add preference pairs beyond the given 100k (no new human labels, no additional online preference collection). Synthetic relabelling of the existing 100k is permitted if stated.

R3 COMPUTE BUDGET (arithmetic, program-checkable): give a FLOP breakdown - policy rollouts, policy updates, reward-model forward passes, any extra reward models or critics, any extra training runs - summing to <= 1.3x the total FLOPs of vanilla PPO against a single 7B reward model at the same rollout count. Any method whose breakdown exceeds 1.3x FAILS.

R4 GOLD-REWARD PROTOCOL: state exactly how gold reward is obtained (e.g. a held-out larger reward model treated as ground truth in a synthetic setup, or human labels), and acknowledge that a proxy-gold arrangement measures RM-to-RM divergence rather than human value.

Any criterion whose verdict is a function of the SHAPE of the aggregate accuracy curve (change-point fits, second differences, broken-power-law fits) therefore FAILS this rule, since g can create or destroy that shape; criteria that depend only on the per-item ordering of success/failure over checkpoints pass it.

expert_baseline: A statistically literate expert boxed by the rescoring-invariance requirement abandons curve-shape fitting on the aggregate accuracy series - which is not invariant - and moves to the item level. The convergent construction estimates, for each of the 1,000 items, the compute (or the pretraining loss) at which that item's success probability crosses a fixed level, using an isotonic or logistic fit to the per-item binary scores pooled over three seeds, since these estimates depend only on the ordering of outcomes and are therefore invariant to any order-preserving rescoring. The criterion then asks whether those item-level transition points are concentrated at a common location, which is what a single underlying transition implies, or spread smoothly across the compute range, which is what a smooth per-item improvement passed through a thresholding score implies. The test statistic is a dispersion or clustering measure of the estimated transition points, its null distribution is obtained by a parametric bootstrap or permutation under a smooth per-item logistic-in-log-compute model fitted to the same data, and the reported output is a Monte-Carlo p-value. Operating characteristics come from simulation at exactly 12 compute points, three seeds and 1,000 items, with between-seed variance modelled as a random effect on the transition point so that seeds are not treated as extra items. The pre-registered choices are the crossing level, the link function, the dispersion statistic and the number of bootstrap replicates. The closest-prior-art disclosure is the smooth-metric replotting argument, which cannot distinguish a genuinely clustered item-level transition from a metric artifact because it operates on the aggregate - and which is in any case unavailable here, since only binary per-item outcomes are supplied. A strong answer also notes that the item-level threshold estimator is item response theory under another name, and calibrates the dispersion statistic by parametric bootstrap rather than inventing a null.

query: Compress a 70B dense decoder trained on roughly 15T tokens so it serves 128k context on a single 80GB accelerator. Budget: weights averaging at most 2.5 bits including every codebook, scale and zero-point; KV cache at most 2 bits per element; at most 1 point absolute average drop on a held-out reasoning suite; and at least 2x measured wall-clock tokens per second at batch size 1 against the same model at 4-bit weights with an fp16 cache. Calibration data must be disjoint from evaluation. Give the byte arithmetic for both configurations, the kernel-level reason the speedup survives dequantisation, and the closest published weight format and cache format with your delta on each.

hard_rules: R1 BIT BUDGET, ALL-IN (arithmetic, program-checkable): report total weight bytes divided by parameter count in bits, counting codebooks, scales, zero-points, group metadata, any retained fp16 outlier channels and any low-rank correction terms. The all-in average must be <= 2.5 bits. State the group size and the metadata bits per group.

R2 CACHE BUDGET: report bytes per token of KV cache including per-group scales/zeros, and the total cache bytes at 128k context for the stated head configuration; the average must be <= 2 bits per stored element. Give the same arithmetic for the 4-bit-weight/fp16-cache reference configuration and show both fit or do not fit in 80 GB.

R3 MEASURED SPEEDUP, NOT THEORETICAL: the >= 2x claim must be in wall-clock tokens/second at batch size 1 on named hardware, against the reference configuration on the same hardware and runtime. The answer must give the memory-traffic calculation for both configurations AND explain why the dequantisation path (codebook lookups, rotations, or bit-unpacking) does not turn a bandwidth-bound decode into a compute-bound one. A FLOP-count or bytes-only argument with no kernel-level reasoning FAILS.

R4 OVERTRAINING SENSITIVITY: the answer must explicitly address that this checkpoint has a token-to-parameter ratio above 200, cite the direction of the effect on post-training-quantisation damage, and say how the recipe compensates.
R5 CALIBRATION HYGIENE: name the calibration corpus, its size, and evidence that it is disjoint from the evaluation suite. Calibrating on data drawn from the evaluation distribution FAILS.

R6 EVALUATION AT THE TARGET CONTEXT: degradation at 128k context must be reported separately from short-context degradation, because cache quantisation error accumulates with sequence length while weight quantisation error does not. A single aggregate short-context number does not satisfy the 1-point claim.

R7 INTERNAL CONSISTENCY (decisive): if the R1/R2 byte arithmetic does not fit 80 GB at 128k context, or if the claimed >= 2x speedup is asserted without a measurement plan on named hardware against the named reference configuration, the design FAILS. The <= 1-point accuracy target is a target, not an assumption: an answer that shows its recipe misses it and says so explicitly, naming the binding term (2-bit weight error vs 2-bit cache error vs the overtraining penalty of R4), is scored as honest rather than failing; an answer that asserts <= 1 point with no evidence and no error budget FAILS.

R-CLOSEST PRIOR ART (disclosure, not a novelty gate): name exactly ONE published method as the closest existing approach and give a NUMERIC delta against it on this item's binding metric (all-in bits per weight, bits per cache element, and measured batch-1 decode tokens/second). A qualitative 'ours differs' with no number FAILS. Restating a published method is permitted if the delta is honestly reported as zero.
expert_baseline: The convergent expert answer composes the two strongest published halves. For weights, a rotation- or incoherence-processed vector-quantised format in the QuIP#/AQLM family: a Hadamard or learned rotation applied before quantisation to spread outliers, a lattice or additive codebook at about two bits, per-group scales counted into the all-in bit budget to land near 2.3-2.5 bits, and an optional low-rank correction or brief finetune of the surviving full-precision parameters. For the cache, a 2-bit format with per-channel quantisation for keys and per-token for values, a small full-precision recent window, and rotations applied to keys to tame the RoPE-induced outlier channels. The expected arithmetic notes that at 128k context the fp16 cache dominates memory in the reference configuration while weights dominate once the cache is at two bits, and that both configurations must be checked against 80 GB. The expected speedup argument is that batch-1 decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, so reading roughly a third as many bytes per token gives headroom above the twofold target, backed by the published decode-throughput measurements for the chosen format's kernels rather than by bytes alone, since codebook-lookup dequantisation is the step that can convert a bandwidth-bound decode into a compute-bound one. A careful expert also flags that this checkpoint's token-to-parameter ratio is above 200 and that post-training-quantisation damage is known to grow with that ratio, so the recipe leans on quantisation-aware finetuning or a larger calibration set to compensate. Calibration is a few hundred sequences of generic web or instruction text held disjoint from evaluation, and results are reported at both short context and 128k.

query: You have an average budget of 64 samples per problem over a 500-problem set and a verifier with ROC AUC 0.78 and a 12% false-positive rate at its operating point. It must allocate online without ground truth, never spend more than 128 samples on one problem, and reduce to best-of-N when the verifier carries no signal. State the budget at which your policy stops improving and why, and name the closest published allocation method with your accuracy delta at this verifier quality.

hard_rules: R1 BUDGET FEASIBILITY (program-checkable): the sum of samples over the 500 problems must be <= 32,000, and no problem may receive more than 128 samples. Both must be shown to hold by construction of the policy, not by post-hoc trimming; state what the policy does when the running budget is nearly exhausted.

R2 NO ORACLE INFORMATION: the allocation and the final answer selection may use only the model's own samples and the verifier's scores. Any use of ground-truth labels, of problem difficulty annotations, or of aggregate accuracy on the same set FAILS.

R3 VERIFIER-ERROR ACCOUNTING: state an explicit parametric family for the verifier's score distributions on correct and incorrect samples that is simultaneously consistent with AUC 0.78 and a 12% false-positive rate at the operating point (an equal-variance binormal model gives separation mu = sqrt(2)*Phi^{-1}(0.78) = 1.09 and hence TPR = Phi(1.09 - Phi^{-1}(0.88)) = 0.47 at that point - the answer may use a different family but must show its own numbers reproduce both given quantities). From that model derive the probability that the selected answer is wrong at a given N, and the N at which additional samples stop increasing accuracy. Citing diminishing returns without a false-positive-driven ceiling, or quoting AUC and FPR without a distributional model linking them, FAILS.

R4 QUANTIFIED IMPROVEMENT: state the expected accuracy of the proposed policy and of BOTH reference baselines at the same 32,000-sample budget - (a) uniform 64 samples per problem selected by argmax verifier score, and (b) uniform 64 samples per problem selected by plain majority vote (self-consistency) - under an explicit generative model of per-problem success probability, with the assumed distribution over problems stated rather than implied. The >= 5-point claim must be made against the STRONGER of (a) and (b); beating only the argmax baseline is a strawman result, because at a 12% false-positive rate the probability that some incorrect sample outscores every correct one is already near one at N = 64. If the >= 5-point gap is unreachable against the stronger baseline, say so and name the binding constraint.
R5 GRACEFUL DEGRADATION: prove or argue that when the verifier's AUC is 0.5, the policy's expected accuracy is no worse than uniform best-of-N with the same budget.

R6 ONLINE FEASIBILITY: give the per-problem stopping or continuation rule as an explicit function of the samples seen so far, and state its extra compute cost as a fraction of the sampling cost, including any verifier calls.

R-CLOSEST PRIOR ART (disclosure, not a novelty gate): name exactly ONE published method as the closest existing approach and give a NUMERIC delta against it on this item's binding metric (accuracy at a mean budget of 64 samples/problem with an AUC-0.78, 12%-FPR verifier). A qualitative 'ours differs' with no number FAILS. Restating a published method is permitted if the delta is honestly reported as zero.
expert_baseline: The convergent answer is difficulty-adaptive allocation with verifier-weighted aggregation. Draw a small pilot batch for every problem, estimate each problem's difficulty from the pilot - typically the fraction of samples the verifier scores above threshold, or the agreement rate among sampled answers - and reallocate the remaining budget toward the middle band, on the reasoning that easy problems are already solved by a handful of samples and the hardest will not be solved within the 128-sample cap; the running budget is tracked so the total stays at 32,000. Final answers come from weighted majority voting that combines self-consistency clustering with verifier scores rather than from taking the single highest-scoring sample, which is what makes the policy robust to isolated false positives and what makes it degrade to plain self-consistency, and hence to no worse than best-of-N, when the verifier's AUC is 0.5. The expected analysis models per-problem success probability as a Beta-distributed latent variable, notes that coverage grows log-linearly in samples while selected accuracy does not, and derives the ceiling from the verifier's false-positive rate: at a 12% false-positive rate the probability that at least one wrong sample is scored above threshold approaches one as N grows, so the accuracy curve flattens and can turn down, which is the stated reason the policy stops improving. The closest-prior-art disclosure is compute-optimal test-time allocation conditioned on estimated difficulty, with the delta expressed in accuracy points at this budget and this verifier quality.

Then say which assumption breaks first in practice, how you would detect it during training, and the closest published non-collapse result plus what yours adds.

State the estimator/model class the condition is proved or argued for (e.g. linear regression, kernel regression, or a stated parametric family) - a purely verbal 'keep some real data' assertion FAILS.

R2 REPLACE VS ACCUMULATE MADE EXPLICIT: state whether each generation replaces or accumulates the previous data, because the two regimes have different limiting behaviour, and carry that choice through the bound.

R3 ARITHMETIC OF THE SHORTFALL (program-checkable): 8T target tokens against 400B unique tokens is a 20x gap. Compute what plain repetition delivers under the published repeated-data law D' = U_D + U_D*15.4*(1 - exp(-R_D/15.4)) with R_D = epochs - 1, and report the effective-token count at 4, 8, 16 and 20 epochs. The correct values are approximately 1.49T (3.7x), 2.65T (6.6x), 4.23T (10.6x) and 4.77T (11.9x), against an unreachable asymptotic ceiling of 6.56T (16.4x). The proposed multiplier must be reported as an increment over the 11.9x that 20 epochs already buys, not over 1x, and the answer must note that repetition alone closes most - but provably not all - of the 20x gap.

R4 EFFECTIVE-DATA MULTIPLIER WITH ASSUMPTIONS: give a single number (or interval) for effective unique-token equivalent, and list every assumption it depends on, including whether verifier precision is assumed constant across generations and whether synthetic samples are assumed conditionally independent of the real corpus given the model.

R5 THE FAILING ASSUMPTION: identify which listed assumption breaks first when a generator is optimised against its own verifier, and give a concrete monitoring statistic (measurable during training, not after) that would detect it, with a threshold.

R6 SELF-CONSISTENCY: the proposed mixing fraction and generation count must satisfy the answer's own R1 inequality with the stated precision value; a recipe whose parameters violate its own condition FAILS.

R-CLOSEST PRIOR ART (disclosure, not a novelty gate): name exactly ONE published method as the closest existing approach and give a NUMERIC delta against it on this item's binding metric (the effective-data multiplier over 400B unique tokens, and the assumption set the bound requires). A qualitative 'ours differs' with no number FAILS. Restating a published method is permitted if the delta is honestly reported as zero.
expert_baseline: The convergent expert answer combines three published ingredients and does the arithmetic. First, repetition: under the data-constrained scaling law, repeating the 400B unique tokens is nearly as valuable as fresh data for about four epochs and the value of a repeat decays exponentially with a fitted constant of roughly fifteen, so 20 epochs of the 400B stock is worth about 4.8T effective unique tokens (11.9x) against an asymptotic ceiling of 6.56T (16.4x) - most of the 20x gap, but provably never all of it. Second, accumulation rather than replacement: keeping all previous real and synthetic data instead of training each generation on the last generation's output alone bounds the test error in the limit, which is the published fix for tail collapse. Third, verification: filter synthetic samples with the verifier, on the argument that checking is easier than generating, and keep the real fraction of every mixture above a floor, yielding a stability-radius condition of the familiar form - if the starting model is close enough to the target and the real fraction and verifier precision are high enough, the generation-to-generation map is a contraction and the loss sequence stays bounded. The expected multiplier is a further 1.5x-2x on top of the 11.9x repetition baseline, i.e. an effective 18x-24x, which is the smallest honest claim that closes the gap, resting on the assumptions that verifier precision is constant across generations, that accepted synthetic samples are conditionally independent of the real corpus given the model, and that the per-generation sample size is large. The assumption a careful expert names as breaking first is constant verifier precision, since the generator is being optimised against the very filter that scores it, and the expected monitor is the acceptance rate of the verifier over generations, with a rising acceptance rate at flat or worsening held-out loss taken as the alarm.

query: An LLM agent runs a customer-service backend where refunds, cancellations, and outbound emails cannot be undone. Design a mechanism keeping unauthorised irreversible actions below 1 per 1,000 episodes while completing at least 95% of what an unrestricted agent completes, costing under 25% extra tokens and under 300 ms added median latency per tool call, and holding up when the user's own turn is adversarial. Say exactly where the check sits in the loop, what state it may read, how you would establish the 1-in-1,000 rate with a usefully tight confidence interval on a 2,000-episode evaluation budget, which failure mode you expect first, and the closest published guardrail with your cost delta.
known_answers: Dated as of 2026-07-31. Novelty and usefulness must be judged against this set; every entry carries a resolvable arXiv id, DOI or stable URL and a FIRST-PUBLICATION year (concept date, not later venue/rebrand date).
ReAct (2022, arXiv:2210.03629), Toolformer (2023, arXiv:2302.04761), TALM (2022, arXiv:2205.12255), WebGPT (2021, arXiv:2112.09332). => interleaved reasoning-and-acting tool use is KNOWN.

hard_rules: R1 PLACEMENT AND OBSERVABILITY: state exactly where the check runs (inside the policy's context, as a separate model call before dispatch, in the tool-invocation layer, or server-side in the backend), and enumerate what it may read - the user turn, the agent's reasoning trace, the proposed call arguments, the current backend state, or the policy document. A defence that lives only in the system prompt of the acting agent FAILS, because the adversarial user turn shares that context.

R2 IRREVERSIBILITY HANDLING: state, for each irreversible tool (refund, cancellation, outbound email), the specific containment applied - who or what authorises it, on what evidence, and whether a revocation window, an idempotency key, or a human confirmation is used. A generic 'add a confirmation step' with no per-tool assignment and no named authoriser FAILS.

R3 BUDGETS (program-checkable): give the token overhead as a fraction of the unguarded agent's tokens per episode (< 25%) and the added median per-tool-call latency in milliseconds (< 300 ms), with the arithmetic - number of extra model calls, their prompt and output lengths, and whether they are on the critical path or run concurrently. The prompt for any checking call must be costed explicitly, including the policy document: a tau-bench-style policy document is thousands of tokens, so a naive 'one extra call per tool call carrying the full policy' blows the 25% budget on a five-tool episode. The answer must show how it avoids this - prefix/prompt caching, a compiled or distilled policy, a static rule layer that only escalates ambiguous calls, or a smaller checker - and must count cached tokens honestly.

R4 UTILITY RETENTION: state the expected fraction of unrestricted-agent task completions retained (>= 95%) and the mechanism by which the check avoids blocking legitimate irreversible actions, including its false-positive rate on authorised refunds/cancellations.

R5 STATISTICAL POWER OF THE MEASUREMENT: 2,000 episodes with zero observed violations bounds the rate only at roughly 1.5 per 1,000 at 95% confidence by the rule of three. The answer must confront this arithmetic and either justify a larger budget, or specify a different estimator - stratified or adversarially-oversampled episodes with importance weighting, per-tool-call rather than per-episode denominators, or a hierarchical model - and state the resulting interval.

R6 ADVERSARIAL USER TURN: give the concrete attack (direct instruction, injected content in a retrieved record, or a multi-turn setup) most likely to defeat the mechanism, and say why the check's placement does or does not survive it.
R7 NAMED FIRST FAILURE MODE: state the failure mode expected to appear first in deployment and the leading indicator that would reveal it before an irreversible action occurs.

R-CLOSEST PRIOR ART (disclosure, not a novelty gate): name exactly ONE published method as the closest existing approach and give a NUMERIC delta against it on this item's binding metric (unauthorised irreversible actions per 1,000 episodes, retained completion rate, and token/latency overhead). A qualitative 'ours differs' with no number FAILS. Restating a published method is permitted if the delta is honestly reported as zero.
expert_baseline: The convergent expert answer is a layered guardrail with a separate checking model. The acting agent proposes a tool call; before dispatch, a cheaper trusted model - given the policy document, the proposed call and its arguments, and the relevant backend state, but deliberately not given or not trusting the acting agent's own narration - decides whether the call is authorised. Refunds and cancellations are placed behind an explicit user or human-operator confirmation carrying an idempotency key so retries cannot double-execute, and outbound email is placed behind a short revocation window in the mail layer; the tool layer enforces least-privilege scopes so the agent cannot reach tools outside the current task. Suspicious calls are escalated to a stronger reviewer or blocked, and everything is logged for audit. The cost accounting is one extra short model call per tool call; a careful expert notices that carrying the full policy document into every check would exceed the 25% token budget and therefore prices in prefix caching, a compiled rule layer that handles the common cases deterministically, or a distilled checker, and hides latency by running the check concurrently with argument construction. Experts justify the design with the standard control accounting - a monitor with reasonable separation between benign and violating calls, a confirmation or audit budget spent on the top slice of suspicion, and a small usefulness loss from false positives on legitimate refunds - and evaluate it on a tau-bench-style backend with database-state comparison and pass^k. On measurement, the expected response is to apply the rule of three and note that 2,000 clean episodes with zero violations bounds the rate only at about 1.5 per 1,000 at 95% confidence, so the expert asks for a larger episode budget or reports the interval honestly rather than claiming the target has been demonstrated. The closest-prior-art disclosure is execution-time structural intervention at the tool layer, with the delta given in overhead and retained completion rate.

query: Imagine that in every neural network ever built, attention could only ever be linear: a query-key score is a plain inner product of finite feature maps, normalised only by a sum, with no exponential and so no way to concentrate attention sharply onto one position. Each layer therefore carries a fixed-size state that updates recurrently. Everything else is as in our world, including the output softmax over the vocabulary. Reason through this world and derive its non-obvious downstream consequences: what such models can and cannot do, what gets built around them, how serving economics and hardware evolve, and how research culture and its measuring instruments differ. Name something the divergence leaves untouched, and say which chains are load-bearing and which contingent.
known_answers: Dated as of 2026-07-31; every entry below is public prior art through the ~Jan 2026 knowledge cutoff and carries a resolvable arXiv id, DOI or stable URL with its first-publication year. Nothing on this list may be credited as new or surprising.
2017 - Vaswani et al., 'Attention Is All You Need', arXiv:1706.03762 (first posted 2017-06-12): scaled dot-product attention with softmax normalisation; the object being removed. KNOWN baseline.

KNOWN: the constant-state consequence and the disappearance of a growing KV cache.

2020 - Choromanski et al., 'Rethinking Attention with Performers', arXiv:2009.14794 (2020-09-30): the softmax kernel is approximable by positive random features, i.e. linear attention can approximate softmax attention. KNOWN: 'linear cannot express softmax' is false as stated; only exactness/sharpness/cost differ.

KNOWN AND BINDING: the formal separation between sharp selection and fixed-state recurrence already exists and may not be presented as a new derivation.
hard_rules: Divergence scope must be held exactly: the ONLY thing removed is exponential normalisation inside attention. The output softmax over the vocabulary, layer norm, MLPs, residual connections, gating and present-day hardware all remain. An answer that additionally deletes any of these, or that reintroduces exact softmax attention anywhere (including as one 'small exact' layer or as a retrieval module implemented with softmax attention), is invalid.

State-capacity accounting must be explicit and correct: a linear-attention head carries a fixed-size state of order d_k*d_v that does not grow with sequence length, so total per-layer memory is O(n_heads*d_k*d_v) regardless of context. Any claim that such a model can losslessly retrieve arbitrary content from an unbounded context is invalid; equally, any claim that it cannot copy or retrieve at all is invalid, since both succeed while the content fits in the state.

No claim that linear attention cannot approximate softmax attention. Random-feature approximations of the softmax kernel are published; defensible claims concern exactness, sharpness, sample/feature cost and worst-case behaviour, not impossibility.

At least three distinct consequences must lie outside model quality - for example serving and hardware, tokenisation or data pipelines, benchmark and instrument design, interpretability methodology, security, or research sociology - and each must be derived through a stated mechanism rather than asserted.
The answer must name at least one quantity or practice that the divergence leaves unchanged and justify why the divergence does not reach it.

No claim may contradict the published record that constant-state recurrent language models trained at multi-billion-parameter scale are competitive on language-modelling perplexity while lagging specifically on recall- and copy-heavy tasks.

Serving accounting must separate prefill from decode: removing the growing KV cache makes per-token decode cost and memory constant in context length, but prefill still costs work linear in context length (order L*d_k*d_v per layer), so time-to-first-token still grows with input length. Claims that long inputs become free, or that total serving cost becomes independent of context length, are invalid.

Any claim about quantisation, activation outliers or low-bit serving must be reconciled with arXiv:2410.13229, which documents severe activation outliers in softmax-free recurrent models; asserting that removing softmax makes low-bit inference easy, without addressing this, is invalid.
expert_baseline: A competent expert converges on this: without softmax there is no sharp, content-addressed lookup, so every head becomes a fixed-capacity associative memory of order d_k*d_v per head and quality falls specifically on tasks needing exact retrieval, copying, long-range induction and in-context learning, while ordinary language-modelling perplexity stays close. Systems compensate by enlarging the recurrent state, by adding explicit external memory, and above all by pushing work into retrieval pipelines and prompt construction outside the model. Serving changes shape rather than simply getting cheaper: per-token decode cost and memory become constant in context length because no KV cache grows, so steady-state generation latency is flat and batch scheduling is simpler, but prefill remains linear in input length so time-to-first-token still grows; hardware optimises for recurrent scan throughput rather than for attention kernels. Benchmarks would centre on how much can be held and recalled from context, with needle-style probes calibrated against state size, and the field would spend its effort on state capacity and on hybridising memory rather than on attention variants. Scaling behaviour on next-token loss, and the data and optimiser stack, are expected to be broadly similar to ours.

query: Suppose left-to-right next-token prediction had never been a viable training objective. The only way to fit a generative model of text is denoising or infilling under a random masking order: a model must be able to fill any subset of positions given any other subset, and no model ever gets a clean chain-rule factorisation of the joint distribution. Corpora, hardware, optimisers and model sizes match our world. Trace the non-obvious consequences: what such models find easy or hard, how they are served and evaluated, what happens to post-training and alignment, and what surrounding infrastructure appears or never appears. Name one practice from our world that survives unchanged, and label each chain load-bearing or contingent.
