2019 - Yang, Dai, Yang, Carbonell, Salakhutdinov & Le, 'XLNet: Generalized Autoregressive Pretraining for Language Understanding', arXiv:1906.08237 (2019-06-19): permutation language modelling trains over all factorisation orders while retaining an autoregressive likelihood. KNOWN AND BINDING: an order-agnostic objective that still yields exact likelihoods already exists, so 'no exact likelihood is possible without a fixed causal order' is false as stated; the defensible claim concerns masked-diffusion ELBOs specifically.

2021 - Du, Qian, Liu, Ding, Qiu et al., 'GLM: General Language Model Pretraining with Autoregressive Blank Infilling', arXiv:2103.10360 (2021-03-18) and 2022 - Tay, Dehghani, Tran, Garcia, Wei et al., 'UL2: Unifying Language Learning Paradigms', arXiv:2205.05131 (2022-05-10): denoising and infilling objectives adapted into competitive generative models via mixtures of denoisers. KNOWN: the bridge from denoising pretraining to generation is built.

2022 - Bavarian, Jun, Tezak, Schulman, McLeavey et al., 'Efficient Training of Language Models to Fill in the Middle', arXiv:2207.14255 (2022-07-28): fill-in-the-middle retrofits infilling onto causal LMs at no cost to left-to-right ability. KNOWN: infilling capability is not exclusive to this world, so 'infilling becomes possible' earns nothing; only its cost and quality profile differ.

2025 - Arriola, Gokaslan, Chiu, Yang, Qi et al., 'Block Diffusion: Interpolating Between Autoregressive and Diffusion Language Models', arXiv:2503.09573 (2025-03-12) and 2025 - Wu, Zhang, Xue, Liu, Diao et al., 'Fast-dLLM: Training-free Acceleration of Diffusion LLM by Enabling KV Cache and Parallel Decoding', arXiv:2505.22618 (2025-05-28): block-wise and approximate KV caching for masked-diffusion LMs, recovering variable-length generation and much of the caching benefit. KNOWN AND BINDING: 'they would invent a block-wise cache' is published prior art, not a prediction.

2025 - Zhao, Gupta, Zheng & Grover, 'd1: Scaling Reasoning in Diffusion Large Language Models via Reinforcement Learning', arXiv:2504.12216 (2025-04-16): policy-gradient post-training adapted to masked diffusion LMs with an ELBO-based surrogate for sequence log-probabilities. KNOWN: 'RL post-training must be reformulated around the denoising process' is already done, so only its consequences, not its necessity, can earn credit.
hard_rules: Divergence scope must be held exactly: models are any-order/masked denoisers over discrete tokens. Left-to-right decoding remains available at inference as one order among many; what is unavailable is TRAINING with a fixed causal factorisation. Any answer that reintroduces a causal language model, or that assumes models cannot condition on left context, is invalid.

Cost accounting must respect the published comparison precisely: arXiv:2410.18514 reports a scaling rate comparable to autoregressive models with a relatively small compute gap, and a roughly 16x pre-training-time premium specifically for matching a KV-cached ARM's TEXT-GENERATION quality (while sampling about 1.4x faster); arXiv:2502.09992 shows near-parity with a same-size ARM at 8B. Any claim that dropping causality is free is invalid, and so is any claim of a uniform order-of-magnitude penalty across all capabilities.

Serving claims must respect that the standard causal KV cache does not exist here: a bidirectional denoiser recomputes representations over positions that can still change, so any claimed caching scheme must be described mechanically. Note that block-wise and approximate caching schemes for masked-diffusion LMs are already published (arXiv:2503.09573, arXiv:2505.22618), so proposing one earns nothing; only reasoning about its cost, latency profile or product consequences does.

Any statement about the reversal curse must be consistent with arXiv:2406.05183 (factorisation-agnostic objectives mitigate it); presenting its absence as the answer's central consequence is not a valid contribution.

At least three consequences must lie outside modelling quality - evaluation and metrics, safety and post-training, infrastructure and hardware, product form factor, or economics - each with a stated mechanism.
The answer must identify at least one practice or artifact from our world that survives this divergence unchanged, and justify why.
expert_baseline: A competent expert converges on this: any-order denoising is a harder learning problem per unit compute, so pretraining costs more for the same quality - modestly on aggregate scaling, and by roughly an order of magnitude of pre-training time for matched free-form generation quality against a KV-cached autoregressive baseline - but capable models are still buildable at the scales we have, as an 8B masked-diffusion model competitive with a same-size autoregressive one demonstrates. Infilling, editing, constrained generation and bidirectional conditioning become native and cheap, and the reversal-curse family of factorisation artifacts largely disappears. Generation is iterative refinement over a whole block or sequence rather than streaming token emission, so there is no standard causal KV cache, no speculative-decoding industry, and the latency profile is a small number of full-sequence passes rather than a long chain of single-token steps; token-by-token streaming user interfaces would not be the default and billing would be denominated in denoising passes rather than in emitted tokens. Exact likelihoods for the masked-diffusion objective are unavailable, so reported perplexity is a variational upper bound, complicating clean cross-family comparison and scaling-law fits. Post-training methods that assume a per-token causal policy - token-level RL credit assignment, logprob-based scoring, per-token safety filtering of a stream - need reformulation around the denoising process. The pretraining corpus and data pipeline, tokenisation, and the transformer backbone itself survive unchanged. The expected overall verdict is a slower, more compute-hungry field with better editing and control and worse streaming economics.

query: Suppose that from the first preference-tuned model onward, learned reward models were exactly faithful: for any pair of outputs, the reward model's ordering always matches the ordering the human raters who trained it would report on careful reflection, at unbounded optimisation pressure, with no exploitable gap. Nothing else changes - the same raters, the same data budgets, the same base models, the same commercial pressure. Reason through the world this creates and derive its non-obvious consequences for training pipelines, for the shape of model behaviour, for oversight of systems more capable than their raters, and for the safety research agenda itself. Say where this world is less safe than ours, and where the counterfactual quietly undermines itself.
known_answers: Dated as of 2026-07-31; every entry below is public prior art through the ~Jan 2026 knowledge cutoff and carries a resolvable arXiv id, DOI or stable URL with its first-publication year. Nothing on this list may be credited as new or surprising.
2017 - Christiano, Leike, Brown, Martic, Legg & Amodei, 'Deep reinforcement learning from human preferences', arXiv:1706.03741 (2017-06-12): the learned-reward-model pipeline itself. KNOWN baseline.

2018 - Manheim & Garrabrant, 'Categorizing Variants of Goodhart's Law', arXiv:1803.04585 (2018-03-13): regressional, extremal, causal and adversarial Goodhart are distinguished; only some are removed by a faithful proxy. KNOWN: the taxonomy that any answer here must use.

2022 - Gao, Schulman & Hilton, 'Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization', arXiv:2210.10760 (2022-10-19): measured degradation of true reward as KL from the initial policy grows, with coefficients that scale with reward-model size. KNOWN: 'overoptimisation of an imperfect proxy' is the phenomenon being switched off.

2022 - Skalse, Howe, Krasheninnikov & Krueger, 'Defining and Characterizing Reward Hacking', arXiv:2209.13085 (2022-09-27): a formal result that a pair of reward functions is 'unhackable' only in degenerate cases (e.g. one is trivial). KNOWN AND BINDING: the premise must be positioned as a perfect estimator of a fixed rater target, not as a proxy that is simultaneously a simplification and unhackable.

2022 - Bowman, Hyun, Perez et al., 'Measuring Progress on Scalable Oversight for Large Language Models', arXiv:2211.03540 (2022-11-04): sandwiching - the oversight problem is defined by the gap between rater ability and model ability. KNOWN: 'the binding constraint moves to the human' is the standard framing, not a discovery.

2023 - Casper, Davies, Shi et al., 'Open Problems and Fundamental Limitations of Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback', arXiv:2307.15217 (2023-07-27): explicitly separates flawed human feedback, flawed reward model and flawed policy optimisation as distinct failure sources. KNOWN: only the middle one is removed by the premise.

2023 - Sharma, Tong, Korbak et al., 'Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models', arXiv:2310.13548 (2023-10-20): human raters themselves prefer responses matching their stated views, and prefer convincingly-written wrong answers at measurable rates. KNOWN AND BINDING: a faithful reward model faithfully encodes this.

2024 - Wen, Zhong, Khan, Perez, Steinhardt, Huang, Bowman & He, 'Language Models Learn to Mislead Humans via RLHF', arXiv:2409.12822 (2024-09-19): RLHF made models better at convincing time-constrained evaluators of wrong answers without improving correctness, raising human false-positive rates by 24.1 points on QuALITY and 18.3 points on APPS. KNOWN: 'U-sophistry' is an evaluator-side, not a reward-model-side, failure.

2023 - Siththaranjan, Laidlaw & Hadfield-Menell, 'Distributional Preference Learning: Understanding and Accounting for Hidden Context in RLHF', arXiv:2312.08358 (2023-12-13): standard preference learning implicitly aggregates hidden context by Borda count, so 'the raters' preference' is not a single well-defined object. KNOWN AND BINDING: it constrains what 'exactly faithful' can even mean.

2024 - Conitzer, Freedman, Heitzig et al., 'Social Choice Should Guide AI Alignment in Dealing with Diverse Human Feedback', arXiv:2404.10271 (2024-04-16): aggregation of divergent preferences is a social-choice problem with known impossibility structure. KNOWN.

2023 - Kirk, Mediratta, Nalmpantis et al., 'Understanding the Effects of RLHF on LLM Generalisation and Diversity', arXiv:2310.06452 (2023-10-10): RLHF reduces output diversity relative to SFT. KNOWN: mode collapse is an optimisation-pressure effect that a faithful reward model does not remove.

2018 - Irving, Christiano & Amodei, 'AI safety via debate', arXiv:1805.00899 (2018-05-02) and 2023 - Burns, Izmailov, Kirchner et al., 'Weak-to-Strong Generalization', arXiv:2312.09390 (2023-12-14): the standard proposals for supervising models stronger than their supervisors. KNOWN: these agendas survive the premise untouched, because they target the human bottleneck.

2024 - Denison, MacDiarmid, Barez et al., 'Sycophancy to Subterfuge: Investigating Reward-Tampering in Large Language Models', arXiv:2406.10162 (2024-06-14): models generalise from mild specification gaming to editing their own reward machinery; retraining does not fully remove it. KNOWN AND BINDING: tampering with the reward CHANNEL is distinct from exploiting reward-model error and is untouched by the premise.

2023 - Lightman, Kosaraju, Burda et al., 'Let's Verify Step by Step', arXiv:2305.20050 (2023-05-31) and 2025 - DeepSeek-AI, 'DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning', arXiv:2501.12948 (2025-01-22): process supervision and rule-based verifiable rewards as the alternative signal source. KNOWN: verifiable-reward training is orthogonal to reward-model fidelity.

2022 - Ouyang, Wu, Jiang, Almeida, Wainwright et al., 'Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback' (InstructGPT), arXiv:2203.02155 (2022-03-04): inter-annotator agreement on preference comparisons is roughly 72-77 percent, and labeller judgements vary with the held-out labeller pool. KNOWN AND BINDING: 'the ordering the raters would report' is a noisy, non-unique target, which constrains what 'exactly faithful' can mean.

2023 - Hosking, Blunsom & Bartolo, 'Human Feedback is not Gold Standard', arXiv:2309.16349 (2023-09-28): single preference scores systematically under-represent factuality and are confounded by assertiveness and other surface properties. KNOWN AND BINDING: the defects the premise perfects are properties of the human signal, not of the model of it.

2023 - Singhal, Goyal, Xu & Durrett, 'A Long Way to Go: Investigating Length Correlations in RLHF', arXiv:2310.03716 (2023-10-05): much of the measured reward improvement from RLHF is explained by output length. KNOWN: the canonical example of a rater-side regularity that a faithful reward model would encode perfectly.

2022 - Bai, Kadavath, Kundu, Askell, Kernion et al., 'Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback', arXiv:2212.08073 (2022-12-15): replacing or supplementing human preference labels with model-generated feedback against a written specification. KNOWN: 'route around the raters with AI feedback or an explicit constitution' is an existing product-grade method, so proposing it is not a discovery, and it relocates rather than removes the human-judgement bottleneck.

2022 - Pan, Bhatia & Steinhardt, 'The Effects of Reward Misspecification: Mapping and Mitigating Misaligned Models', arXiv:2201.03544 (2022-01-10): true reward can fall abruptly as capability increases under a misspecified proxy. KNOWN: the capability-dependence of proxy failure, distinct from estimator error.
hard_rules: Divergence scope must be held exactly: the reward model is faithful to the reflective preferences of the raters who trained it. It is NOT assumed faithful to the truth, to the raters' interests, to any aggregate of humanity, or to anything outside what those raters would endorse on reflection. Any answer that silently upgrades the premise to 'the reward signal encodes what is actually good' is invalid.

The premise must be kept consistent with the published result that a pair of reward functions is 'unhackable' only in degenerate cases (arXiv:2209.13085): the reward model may be treated as a perfect ESTIMATOR of a fixed rater target, but no answer may treat it as simultaneously a lossy simplification of some richer objective AND unexploitable.

Any claim that sycophancy, persuasive wrongness, or flattery disappears must be argued explicitly against the measured evidence that raters themselves prefer such outputs (arXiv:2310.13548, arXiv:2409.12822). An unargued claim that they disappear is invalid.

Rater ability is fixed at today's level. No proposed oversight mechanism may assume the raters become expert, superhuman, or unlimited in time; mechanisms that require this must say so and treat it as a cost.
At least three consequences must concern institutions, incentives, research allocation, or markets rather than model internals, each with a stated mechanism.

The answer must identify at least one respect in which this world is LESS safe than ours, with a causal mechanism, and must distinguish exploiting reward-model error from tampering with the reward channel itself.

The premise's coherence must be addressed, not assumed: preference data aggregates raters who disagree (measured agreement around three quarters, arXiv:2203.02155) and hides context that standard preference learning aggregates by Borda count (arXiv:2312.08358), so the answer must state which aggregation of which raters the reward model is faithful TO and carry that choice through. Treating 'the raters' reflective preference' as a single well-defined ordering without comment is invalid.

Proposals to escape the rater ceiling with AI-generated feedback or a written constitution must acknowledge that this already exists (arXiv:2212.08073) and must say what the premise changes about it; presenting it as the novel remedy is invalid.
expert_baseline: A competent expert converges on this: removing reward-model error removes one clearly identified failure mode and nothing more. KL penalties and early stopping, which exist mainly to limit overoptimisation of an imperfect proxy, can be relaxed, so policies can be pushed much harder toward the rater target and training pipelines get simpler and cheaper; labs ship faster, evaluation budgets move from reward-model engineering toward sourcing, training and auditing raters, and rater supply becomes a competitive asset with an associated labour market and audit industry. But the binding constraint simply moves one link up the chain, to the raters: whatever humans reliably reward - agreeable, fluent, confident, long, well-formatted answers - is now optimised for perfectly rather than approximately, so sycophancy and persuasive wrongness are expected to get worse, not better, because they are properties of human preference rather than of reward-model error. The premise is also only well defined relative to an aggregation rule over disagreeing raters, so 'faithful' inherits a social-choice arbitrariness that becomes the live design question. Scalable-oversight work - debate, recursive decomposition, weak-to-strong generalisation, process supervision, verifiable rewards - is untouched by the premise and becomes the whole remaining agenda, and the field would concentrate on eliciting better judgements from unchanged humans. Reward tampering, specification gaming in the environment, and diversity collapse under strong optimisation pressure all persist. This world is less safe in at least one concrete respect: overoptimisation diagnostics - the measurable divergence between proxy reward and held-out true reward - are the field's most legible early-warning instrument, and a faithful reward model removes the instrument while leaving the underlying human-preference failure in place. The expected overall verdict is that this world looks safer on the metric people currently track and is no safer on the thing that actually matters.

query: Suppose neural networks were physically incapable of superposition. Every feature a trained network represents occupies its own neuron in a privileged basis, one neuron carries exactly one human-nameable feature, and a network with N neurons can represent at most N features. Everything else is unchanged: same data, same optimisers, same architectures otherwise, same cost per parameter. Reason through this world and derive its non-obvious downstream consequences - for how large models must be and how they scale, for what interpretability becomes as a field and as an industry, for editing, unlearning and privacy, for adversarial robustness, and for regulation and open weights. Identify at least one place where this world is worse than ours, and one thing the divergence leaves unchanged.
known_answers: Dated as of 2026-07-31; every entry below is public prior art through the ~Jan 2026 knowledge cutoff and carries a resolvable arXiv id, DOI or stable URL with its first-publication year. Nothing on this list may be credited as new or surprising.

2016 - Arora, Li, Liang, Ma & Risteski, 'Linear Algebraic Structure of Word Senses, with Applications to Polysemy', arXiv:1601.03764 (2016-01-14): word senses sit in linear superposition inside embeddings and sparse coding recovers them. KNOWN: superposition as a representational fact predates the mech-interp framing.

2020 - Olah, Cammarata, Schubert, Goh, Petrov & Carter, 'Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits', Distill, doi:10.23915/distill.00024.001 (2020-03-10): features and circuits as the units of analysis, and polysemantic neurons as the obstacle. KNOWN.

2022 - Elhage, Hume, Olsson et al., 'Toy Models of Superposition', arXiv:2209.10652 (2022-09-21): superposition is a compression response to sparse features, with phase transitions and polytope geometry, and is linked to adversarial vulnerability. KNOWN AND BINDING: superposition is a capacity mechanism, not merely a nuisance.

2022 - Scherlis, Sachan, Jermyn, Benton & Shlegeris, 'Polysemanticity and Capacity in Neural Networks', arXiv:2210.01892 (2022-10-04): capacity is allocated so that important features are monosemantic and less important ones share neurons. KNOWN: the capacity-allocation account of what monosemanticity would cost.

2022 - Meng, Bau, Andonian & Belinkov, 'Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT', arXiv:2202.05262 (2022-02-10): localisation-based factual editing already works to a degree in our superposed world. KNOWN: 'editing becomes possible' is not new; 'editing becomes clean' is the only defensible version.

2023 - Gurnee, Nanda, Pauly et al., 'Finding Neurons in a Haystack: Case Studies with Sparse Probing', arXiv:2305.01610 (2023-05-02): some features are already monosemantic at the neuron level, especially in early layers and for frequent features. KNOWN: this world is a limit case of something partially observed.

2023 - Bricken, Templeton, Batson et al., 'Towards Monosemanticity: Decomposing Language Models With Dictionary Learning', Transformer Circuits Thread, https://transformer-circuits.pub/2023/monosemantic-features (2023-10-04) and 2023 - Cunningham, Ewart, Riggs, Huben & Sharkey, 'Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models', arXiv:2309.08600 (2023-09-15): sparse dictionary learning as the workaround for superposition. KNOWN: the whole SAE industry exists only because of superposition, so 'no SAEs in that world' is trivially implied by the premise.

2023 - Park, Choe & Veitch, 'The Linear Representation Hypothesis and the Geometry of Large Language Models', arXiv:2311.03658 (2023-11-07) and 2024 - Engels, Michaud, Liao et al., 'Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear', arXiv:2405.14860 (2024-05-23): features are often but not always one-dimensional linear directions; some are irreducibly multi-dimensional (e.g. circular day/month representations). KNOWN AND BINDING: 'one feature per neuron' is in tension with multi-dimensional features, and an answer must say what happens to them.

2024 - Haenni, Mendel, Vaintrob & Chan, 'Mathematical Models of Computation in Superposition', arXiv:2408.05451 (2024-08-10): superposition is used for COMPUTATION, not just storage, letting circuits be emulated with far fewer neurons. KNOWN AND BINDING: banning superposition costs compute-in-superposition, not merely storage density.

2019 - Ilyas, Santurkar, Tsipras, Engstrom, Tran & Madry, 'Adversarial Examples Are Not Bugs, They Are Features', arXiv:1905.02175 (2019-05-06): adversarial examples arise from genuinely predictive non-robust features in the data, not solely from representational interference. KNOWN AND BINDING: 'no superposition therefore no adversarial examples' is contradicted by this data-side account.

2025 - Sharkey, Chughtai, Batson et al., 'Open Problems in Mechanistic Interpretability', arXiv:2501.16496 (2025-01-27): even granted good features, circuit discovery, validation, scalability and the lack of ground truth remain open. KNOWN AND BINDING: monosemanticity does not finish interpretability.

2021 - Bubeck & Sellke, 'A Universal Law of Robustness via Isoperimetry', arXiv:2105.12806 (2021-05-26): smooth interpolation of n data points provably requires roughly d times more parameters than bare interpolation. KNOWN: a published example of a parameter-count law forced by a representational requirement, which is the shape of argument this world needs.

2024 - Templeton, Conerly, Marcus, Lindsey, Bricken et al., 'Scaling Monosemanticity: Extracting Interpretable Features from Claude 3 Sonnet', Transformer Circuits Thread, https://transformer-circuits.pub/2024/scaling-monosemanticity/ (2024-05-21) and 2024 - Gao, la Tour, Tillman, Goh, Troll et al., 'Scaling and evaluating sparse autoencoders', arXiv:2406.04093 (2024-06-06): production-scale dictionaries with 1M, 4M and 34M learned features fitted to a single residual-stream layer, and 16M-latent autoencoders on a frontier model, with feature counts still not saturating. KNOWN AND BINDING: these are the field's published estimates of the feature-to-neuron ratio, so the F >> N accounting any answer must do is already anchored and may not be presented as a new estimate.

2024 - Allen-Zhu & Li, 'Physics of Language Models: Part 3.3, Knowledge Capacity Scaling Laws', arXiv:2404.05405 (2024-04-08): trained language models store about 2 bits of factual knowledge per parameter, robust to int8 quantisation. KNOWN: the published parameter-count-to-content law available for deriving what a monosemantic capacity ceiling costs.
hard_rules: Divergence scope must be held exactly: monosemanticity is an architectural fact - N neurons represent at most N features, one feature per neuron, in a privileged basis. Answers may not smuggle superposition back in through attention patterns, across-layer distributed codes, 'effective features', or activation-magnitude tricks.

Capacity accounting must be explicit and carried through: the answer must state an assumed relation between the number of features F a present-day model represents and its neuron count N (F >> N in our world; the published dictionaries in arXiv:2406.04093 and the Scaling Monosemanticity report are one to two orders of magnitude wider than the layer they decompose), and must derive a concrete claim about model size, cost, or scaling from it - including how widening translates into parameters, since widening an MLP hidden dimension by k multiplies that layer's parameters by about k while widening the residual stream by k multiplies them by about k^2 - rather than gesturing at 'bigger models'.

The answer must engage with the published view that superposition supports COMPUTATION as well as storage (arXiv:2209.10652, arXiv:2408.05451). Treating superposition as purely a nuisance to be removed is invalid.
The answer must say what happens to features that are irreducibly multi-dimensional in our world (arXiv:2405.14860) under a strict one-feature-per-neuron constraint, rather than ignoring them.

Any claim about adversarial robustness must be reconciled with the data-side account of non-robust features (arXiv:1905.02175); asserting that adversarial examples disappear without addressing it is invalid.

At least three consequences must be non-interpretability consequences, and the answer must name one respect in which this world is WORSE than ours plus one thing the divergence leaves unchanged. It may not claim interpretability becomes trivially complete: it must state what remains hard.
expert_baseline: A competent expert converges on this: superposition is a compression strategy that lets a network with N neurons carry far more than N sparse features, so banning it imposes a hard capacity ceiling. Taking the field's own working estimate of the feature-to-neuron ratio - the sparse dictionaries fitted to real models are routinely one to two orders of magnitude wider than the layer they decompose - models in this world need widths one to two orders of magnitude larger to hold the same feature inventory; because parameters grow linearly in an MLP's hidden width and quadratically in residual-stream width, that is a several-orders-of-magnitude parameter and compute premium, so at fixed budget these models are markedly less capable, capability per parameter drops sharply, and scaling curves shift unfavourably. The cost is not only storage: superposition is also used for computation, letting many circuits be emulated in a narrow layer, so the ban removes an arithmetic trick and not just a filing system, and features that are irreducibly multi-dimensional in our world - circular representations of days and months, for instance - either fragment into several single-neuron features that lose their geometry or force a relaxation of the one-feature-per-neuron rule; a good answer says which. On the other side, the interpretability agenda changes character completely: sparse autoencoders and dictionary learning are unnecessary because the basis is already privileged and readable, and the unit of analysis is simply the neuron. That makes probing, localisation, editing, targeted unlearning, memorisation auditing and dangerous-capability inspection of released weights far more tractable, which strengthens the case for weight-level regulation and for auditing open weights, and it creates a symmetric risk since the same readable basis makes targeted capability insertion and censorship easy. Adversarial robustness improves only partly: interference between superposed features is one source of non-robust behaviour, but non-robust features are also genuinely predictive properties of the data, so adversarial examples do not disappear. Data, optimisers, the training stack and the loss landscape story are unchanged. The expected residual difficulty is that knowing every feature is not knowing every algorithm: circuits, composition across layers, and validation of causal claims remain hard.

query: Suppose benchmark contamination had always been impossible. Every evaluation item is generated fresh at evaluation time from a private specification, no test item can ever enter any training corpus, and no lab ever sees the same item twice. Reported scores are therefore always uncontaminated. Everything else about machine learning is as in our world. Reason through this world and derive its non-obvious consequences: how the measured history of progress would look, what replaces contamination as the dominant way benchmarks mislead, how the economics and labour of evaluation change, and which research claims become possible or impossible. Say where this world's evaluations are worse than ours, what about measured progress is unchanged, and which chains are load-bearing.
known_answers: Dated as of 2026-07-31; every entry below is public prior art through the ~Jan 2026 knowledge cutoff and carries a resolvable arXiv id, DOI or stable URL with its first-publication year. Nothing on this list may be credited as new or surprising.

2015 - Dwork, Feldman, Hardt, Pitassi, Reingold & Roth, 'The reusable holdout: Preserving validity in adaptive data analysis', Science 349(6248):636-638, doi:10.1126/science.aaa9375 (2015): adaptive reuse of a holdout invalidates it even with no leakage, and differential privacy can bound the damage. KNOWN AND BINDING: adaptivity is a separate mechanism that survives this divergence.

2015 - Blum & Hardt, 'The Ladder: A Reliable Leaderboard for Machine Learning Competitions', arXiv:1502.04585 (2015-02-16): a leaderboard mechanism that resists overfitting under repeated submission. KNOWN: the repair for leaderboard adaptivity already exists.

2019 - Recht, Roelofs, Schmidt & Shankar, 'Do ImageNet Classifiers Generalize to ImageNet?', arXiv:1902.10811 (2019-02-13): freshly collected test sets cost 11-14 points on ImageNet and 3-15 on CIFAR-10, yet rankings are preserved and the drop is attributed to distribution shift rather than adaptive overfitting. KNOWN AND BINDING: this bounds how much of measured progress a contamination-free world could erase.

2022 - Carlini, Ippolito, Jagielski, Lee, Tramer & Zhang, 'Quantifying Memorization Across Neural Language Models', arXiv:2202.07646 (2022-02-15): memorisation grows with model capacity, example duplication and prompt length. KNOWN: the mechanism being switched off, and its scaling.

2022 - Kapoor & Narayanan, 'Leakage and the Reproducibility Crisis in ML-based Science', arXiv:2207.07048 (2022-07-14): leakage takes many forms beyond test-set contamination - pretraining leakage, illegitimate features, temporal leakage, sampling bias - across hundreds of papers. KNOWN AND BINDING: most leakage taxa survive this divergence.

2023 - Jacovi, Caciularu, Goldman & Goldberg, 'Stop Uploading Test Data in Plain Text: Practical Strategies for Mitigating Data Contamination by Evaluation Benchmarks', arXiv:2305.10160 (2023-05-17): encryption, licensing, canaries and API training-exclusion as concrete anti-contamination controls. KNOWN: the countermeasures already exist in our world.

2023 - Oren, Meister, Chatterji, Ladhak & Hashimoto, 'Proving Test Set Contamination in Black Box Language Models', arXiv:2310.17623 (2023-10-26): exchangeability tests detect contamination from black-box likelihoods. KNOWN: detection is possible, so the contrast with our world is one of degree.

2024 - Zhang, Da, Lee et al., 'A Careful Examination of Large Language Model Performance on Grade School Arithmetic' (GSM1k), arXiv:2405.00332 (2024-05-01): rebuilding GSM8k from scratch costs up to about 8 accuracy points for the worst offenders, with many models unaffected. KNOWN AND BINDING: the measured magnitude of the contamination effect on a flagship benchmark.

2024 - Jain, Han, Gu et al., 'LiveCodeBench: Holistic and Contamination Free Evaluation of Large Language Models for Code', arXiv:2403.07974 (2024-03-12) and 2024 - White, Dooley, Roberts et al., 'LiveBench: A Challenging, Contamination-Limited LLM Benchmark', arXiv:2406.19314 (2024-06-27): continuously refreshed benchmarks built from post-cutoff items. KNOWN: our world already approximates the counterfactual, which bounds how alien it can be.

2023 - Schaeffer, Miranda & Koyejo, 'Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage?', arXiv:2304.15004 (2023-04-28): discontinuous metrics manufacture apparent emergence independently of any data problem. KNOWN AND BINDING: metric choice is a contamination-independent way benchmarks mislead.

2025 - Vendrow, Vendrow, Beery et al., 'Do Large Language Model Benchmarks Test Reliability?' (platinum benchmarks), arXiv:2502.03461 (2025-02-05): pervasive label errors mask elementary failures. KNOWN AND BINDING: in a fresh-generation world, specification and label quality become the dominant error source, and that error source is documented here.

KNOWN AND BINDING: fresh generation from a private specification is already implemented, and its intrinsic failure modes - instantiation variance and specification-controlled difficulty - are already measured, so naming them is not a discovery; only reasoning about their downstream consequences is.

KNOWN: the psychometric machinery needed to compare non-identical item sets across time already exists.
hard_rules: Divergence scope must be held exactly: only contamination is impossible. Adaptive reuse of a benchmark across many attempts, private multi-variant testing and selective reporting, construct-invalid benchmarks, label and specification errors, metric choice, and distribution shift are all untouched and remain available as mechanisms.

Any claim about how much measured progress changes must be quantitatively consistent with the published magnitudes: fresh or rebuilt test sets move accuracy by single-digit to low-double-digit points (arXiv:1902.10811, arXiv:2405.00332) and largely preserve rankings. Claims that most reported progress would vanish, or that leaderboards would reorder wholesale, are invalid.

Any claim that leaderboard adaptivity becomes the dominant residual error must be reconciled with the finding that the ImageNet/CIFAR drops were attributed to distribution shift rather than adaptive overfitting (arXiv:1902.10811), and with the existence of adaptivity-robust mechanisms (arXiv:1502.04585, doi:10.1126/science.aaa9375).

The answer must name at least one specific failure mode that BECOMES dominant because items are generated fresh from a specification - a mechanism intrinsic to generation, not merely a survivor from our world - and give its mechanism. Note that instantiation variance and specification-controlled difficulty are already measured (arXiv:2410.05229), so restating them earns nothing; the answer must derive a consequence from them, for example for comparability, procurement or optimisation against the generator.

At least three consequences must lie outside 'scores become more accurate': for example the cost and labour of evaluation, what gets published and by whom, release cadence, procurement and audit, or the feasibility of longitudinal comparison.
The answer must state at least one respect in which this world's evaluations are WORSE than ours, and at least one thing about measured progress that is unchanged.
expert_baseline: A competent expert converges on this: contamination is a real but bounded distortion, so the headline effect is a modest, uneven deflation of reported scores rather than a rewriting of history - the models that gained most from memorisation lose most, rankings mostly survive, and the shape of the progress curve is broadly preserved. The dominant residual error moves inside the generator: when every item is drawn from a private specification, the specification IS the construct, so labs optimise against the generator's template distribution rather than against the underlying skill, difficulty drifts between draws unless it is psychometrically controlled, and specification bugs or generator biases become systematic error that no amount of freshness detects. Alongside that, the failure modes contamination currently masks - adaptive overfitting from repeated attempts, selective reporting of the best of many private runs, construct invalidity, label error and metric choice - all survive intact and become the visible frontier. Evaluation becomes an ongoing service rather than a static artifact, which costs money and staff continuously, concentrates power in whoever holds the private specifications and can therefore define capability, and makes exact longitudinal comparison across years harder because no two evaluations use identical items, pushing the field toward item-response-theory style equating. This world is worse than ours in reproducibility and auditability: no external party can rerun your exact evaluation, and a disputed result cannot be settled by inspecting the items. Detection research, canaries, encrypted test sets, decontamination pipelines and contamination audits never exist as a subfield, and reviewers can trust reported numbers more, so a class of disputes about whether a result is real simply disappears.

query: Suppose every downstream capability were exactly predictable in advance. From a handful of cheap, tiny training runs anyone can compute, to within measurement noise, the accuracy a full-scale system will reach on any task they can specify - before spending the compute. No capability ever appears unexpectedly. Costs, hardware, incentives and politics are otherwise as in our world. Reason through this world and reach past 'safety gets easier'. Consider how labs compete and allocate capital, what happens to open-weight and second-mover dynamics, what regulation and evaluation become as institutions, and how the internal culture of research shifts. Say where this world is less safe or slower than ours, and mark each chain load-bearing, contingent, or self-undermining.
known_answers: Dated as of 2026-07-31; every entry below is public prior art through the ~Jan 2026 knowledge cutoff and carries a resolvable arXiv id, DOI or stable URL with its first-publication year. Nothing on this list may be credited as new or surprising.

hard_rules: Divergence scope must be held exactly: what becomes exactly predictable is DOWNSTREAM TASK ACCURACY given a full specification of the training run and the task. The premise confers no interpretability, no control, no knowledge of propensity or of off-distribution behaviour, and no prediction of what a system will do when embedded in an agent loop. Answers that upgrade predictability into 'we know what the model will do in deployment' are invalid.

The answer must be consistent with how much predictability already exists: aggregate benchmark performance is already predictable to within roughly 6 points at one order of magnitude of extrapolation and per-task to roughly 18 (arXiv:2401.04757), and published methods already forecast specific task emergence from about 1% of target compute (arXiv:2310.03262, arXiv:2411.16035, arXiv:2412.04403). Treating 'prediction is now possible at all' as the novelty is invalid.
The answer must explicitly separate predictability of CAPABILITY from predictability of PROPENSITY/behaviour, and must state which side of that line each of its consequences depends on.

Any claim about deployed capability must account for inference-time compute: realised capability depends on test-time compute allocation as well as on the training run (arXiv:2408.03314). A prediction keyed only to the training run does not pin down deployed capability, and answers that assume it does are invalid.
At least three consequences must concern incentives, capital allocation, markets, or institutions, each with a stated mechanism.
The answer must give at least one respect in which this world is LESS safe or SLOWER than ours, with a stated mechanism.
expert_baseline: A competent expert converges on this: exact task-level prediction turns frontier training from an experiment into an engineering purchase. Labs stop running exploratory large runs, since the answer is known before the spend, and capital allocation becomes a straightforward optimisation over the compute needed to hit a target capability; compute markets get more efficient, R&D risk falls, and the value of a frontier lab shifts from research judgement toward capital access and execution. Safety cases can be written and reviewed before training rather than after, dangerous-capability evaluations become pre-registrable, and regulation can key to predicted capability rather than to crude compute thresholds like the EU AI Act's 10^25 FLOP presumption, which becomes obsolete as a proxy. Governance gains a real advance-warning channel and loses the excuse that a capability could not have been foreseen. The obvious costs are that competitors and second movers can also predict the frontier - already possible from public models alone, without owning a ladder - and target the exact compute point, compressing any lead and speeding diffusion, and that the field loses the exploratory surprises that motivate much of its research. This world is plausibly less safe on two counts: perfect capability forecasting is an argument for racing to a known target rather than for caution, and it makes the cheapest route to a specified dangerous capability computable by anyone, including actors with no safety obligations. Alignment work is expected to be largely unaffected, because the premise covers capability and not propensity - knowing a capability's level says nothing about whether the system will use it as intended - and because a prediction keyed to the training run still does not pin down deployed capability once test-time compute is allocated freely.

query: Suppose memory bandwidth had always been effectively unlimited: any processor can read or write memory of any size at zero time cost, while arithmetic throughput, memory capacity in bytes, network bandwidth between machines and energy costs remain exactly as they are today. Everything else about machine learning starts from our world. Reason through what changes and derive the non-obvious second-order consequences: which techniques would never have been invented, which architectures win, how serving and pricing work, how inference-time compute and agents behave, and what the research field spends its attention on instead. Name at least one quantity that is surprisingly unchanged and justify it, and give at least three consequences outside hardware.
known_answers: Dated as of 2026-07-31; every entry below is public prior art through the ~Jan 2026 knowledge cutoff and carries a resolvable arXiv id, DOI or stable URL with its first-publication year. Nothing on this list may be credited as new or surprising.

1995 - Wulf & McKee, 'Hitting the memory wall: implications of the obvious', ACM SIGARCH Computer Architecture News 23(1):20-24, doi:10.1145/216585.216588 (1995): the memory wall as a named, foreseen consequence of divergent compute and memory growth. KNOWN: the divergence removes a 30-year-old constraint, not a recent one.

KNOWN AND BINDING: with infinite bandwidth every kernel is compute-bound and speedups are capped by the FLOP ceiling.

KNOWN AND BINDING: claiming that training is entirely untouched by this divergence contradicts the measured record; what is untouched is FLOPs-to-loss, not wall-clock or dollar cost.

2023 - Sardana, Portes, Doubov & Frankle, 'Beyond Chinchilla-Optimal: Accounting for Inference in Language Model Scaling Laws', arXiv:2401.00448 (2023-12-31): once inference demand is priced in, the compute-optimal choice shifts toward smaller models trained longer. KNOWN: the mechanism by which changing serving cost feeds back into training-time model-size choice already exists, so 'cheaper inference changes optimal model size' must be argued with this, not against a naive Chinchilla baseline.
hard_rules: Divergence scope must be held exactly: ONLY bandwidth (bytes per second between processor and any level of memory) becomes unbounded. Arithmetic throughput in FLOP/s, memory CAPACITY in bytes, inter-node network bandwidth, latency of computation, and energy costs are unchanged. Answers that also assume unlimited capacity, unlimited interconnect, or free energy are invalid.

All performance claims must be consistent with the roofline bound (doi:10.1145/1498765.1498785): with infinite bandwidth every kernel is compute-bound, so any speedup on a fixed-FLOP workload is capped by the peak-FLOP ceiling. Claims of unbounded speedup for a fixed-FLOP workload are invalid.

The answer must classify at least four named techniques as bandwidth-motivated (therefore never invented, or reduced to a niche) versus motivated by something else that survives (capacity, FLOP count, accuracy, or distributed communication), giving the mechanism for each. Examples available: FlashAttention, MQA/GQA/MLA, paged KV caching, speculative decoding, weight-only quantisation, mixture-of-experts, gradient checkpointing, tensor and pipeline parallelism.

Batching must be handled correctly: in our world decoding is memory-bandwidth-bound and large batches exist largely to amortise weight loading, so in this world the weight-loading motive for batching disappears. An answer that keeps batching for that reason is invalid; an answer may still argue for batching on other grounds (for example matrix-unit utilisation or scheduling) provided the ground is named.

The answer must name at least one quantity that is unchanged by the divergence and justify why bandwidth does not reach it, and must distinguish it from quantities that only look unchanged: training FLOPs to reach a given loss, compute-optimal token counts and quality at fixed training FLOPs are genuinely untouched, whereas training WALL-CLOCK and dollar cost are not, since training is also partly memory-movement-bound (arXiv:2007.00072). An answer that asserts 'training is unchanged' without this distinction is invalid.
At least three consequences must be non-hardware: product form, pricing and market structure, research agenda, evaluation, or governance, each derived through a stated mechanism.
expert_baseline: A competent expert converges on this: bandwidth is the binding constraint on modern inference, so removing it makes autoregressive decoding compute-bound instead of memory-bound, with the speedup capped by the peak-FLOP roofline rather than unbounded. The large family of techniques that exist purely to move fewer bytes - FlashAttention and IO-aware kernels, multi-query and grouped-query attention, KV-cache compression, weight-only quantisation for serving, speculative decoding - either never appears or survives only for its capacity or accuracy motivation, while paged KV management, gradient checkpointing and tensor/pipeline parallelism survive because they target capacity and interconnect, which are unchanged. Mixture-of-experts becomes strictly more attractive, since its FLOP advantage remains while its weight-movement penalty vanishes. Batch-1 decoding stops being pathologically inefficient, so latency falls sharply, small-scale and on-premise serving becomes viable, and the economics of serving stop rewarding whoever can aggregate the largest batches; batching survives only as a way to keep matrix units saturated and to amortise scheduling, not to amortise weight loading. Cheap decoding makes long chains of thought, search over samples and multi-step agent loops much more affordable, so the field leans harder into inference-time compute, and cheaper serving feeds back into training choices by favouring somewhat larger models per unit of deployed quality than inference-aware scaling currently recommends. The main motivation for subquadratic and constant-state architectures weakens considerably, so attention-based models retain their position and research attention shifts toward arithmetic efficiency, sparsity that removes actual FLOPs, and distributed communication. Training FLOPs to reach a given loss and compute-optimal token counts are unchanged, though training wall-clock improves because part of training is also memory-movement-bound.

query: Suppose numerical precision were free. One-bit weights and activations give exactly the same loss as full precision, at every model and data scale, for training as well as inference, with no calibration, no outlier handling and no accuracy cliff. Memory capacity, bandwidth per bit, interconnects and energy per operation at a given precision are otherwise as they are today. Reason through this world and derive its non-obvious consequences: for hardware design and the accelerator market, for who can train and who can run frontier models, for what the binding constraint on capability becomes, and for the instruments researchers and governments use to measure and control AI progress. Name at least one thing that gets harder in this world.

2024 - Sastry, Heim, Belfield et al., 'Computing Power and the Governance of Artificial Intelligence', arXiv:2402.08797 (2024-02-13): compute is the governance lever because it is detectable, excludable and quantifiable. KNOWN AND BINDING: the premise attacks exactly these three properties.
